paras: The threatened lynching of Emanuel Johnson took place in Maury County, Tennessee, in November 1880, after Johnson, a Black railroad section hand, was accused of shooting and killing his white foreman, John Booth, who had discharged him. Newspapers predicted that Johnson would be lynched, and one reported that a lynching party had been organized at Columbia, but no report shows that he was harmed.

Booth was foreman of section 8 on the Nashville & Decatur division of the railroad, and Johnson had worked under him until Booth discharged him. According to the Pulaski Citizen, Johnson came to where the hands were working at Campbell's station, insulted Booth, drew a pistol and shot him just above the heart, and Booth died almost at once. A Cincinnati dispatch dated November 20 put the shooting on the previous day, while two Tennessee weeklies dated it to the Thursday before, November 18.

The first reports, from a Columbia special to the Cincinnati Commercial, said that Johnson, "if caught, will be lynched." On November 22 the Wilmington Daily Republican added that Johnson had eluded arrest at last accounts. The next day the Wheeling Register stated that "a lynching party has been organized at Columbia."

The Pulaski Citizen, the fullest account, reported that Johnson had been arrested and placed in the Columbia jail. It described the people about Campbell's station as "greatly excited" and said that for a while there was talk of going to Columbia to lynch him, without reporting that anyone did so.
No later report of Johnson's fate, an inquest on Booth, an indictment or a trial was found in the coverage.

The story reached readers mainly through the short Cincinnati wire, printed between November 20 and 25 in Washington, Knoxville, Richmond and Concord, New Hampshire, usually as one item in a crime roundup ending with the lynching prediction. The Richmond Dispatch headed it "A Section-Hand Kills his Foreman for Discharging Him," and the Lancaster Intelligencer set it under "MURDEROUS NEGROES" beside an unrelated Kentucky killing, with the subhead "Emanuel Johnson's Revenge." Tennessee weeklies in Pulaski and Fayetteville gave local detail; the Pulaski Citizen called Johnson "the scoundrel," and the Fayetteville Observer wrote that it was feared he would be lynched. None of the papers commented on the prospect of a lynching.

Accounts differ on whether Johnson was at large or in jail when the threat was made: the wire and the Wilmington paper described him as uncaught, while the later Pulaski report placed him in the Columbia jail. Only the Wheeling Register said a lynching party had actually organized, whereas the nearer Pulaski account described only talk.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Emanuel Johnson
bases: Papers reported that Johnson would be lynched if caught, that a lynching party had organized at Columbia, and that people near Campbell's station talked of going to Columbia to lynch him; no attack was reported (A2, A8, A9).

The coverage reports only a threat: a predicted lynching, an organized 'lynching party' (Wheeling only) and talk of going to the Columbia jail, with no report that Johnson was harmed (A2, A8, A9). The threat was framed as retribution for the alleged killing of Booth (A2, A9).

The Cincinnati wire (A2, A5) and the independent Pulaski Citizen account (A9) agree that Johnson was accused of killing Booth after being discharged and that he faced a lynching threat; only Wheeling (A8) says a party was actually organized.
